rv.q: But the star is Channing: there is nowhere for her to hide and she is quite brilliant.
Nevertheless, Apologia is always strongly acted, often funny and with some memorably acerbic one-liners, and it’s given the usual dynamic direction by Jamie Lloyd.
If, as tables are turned, this absorbing, finely acted evening leaves a pronounced taste of standard-issue “progressive” seasoning in the mouth, there’s still plenty enough to chew on before that.
Too much of Alexi Kaye Campbell’s drama runs on automatic pilot: on the well-worn set-up of a family reunion exploding.
It’s a solid production from a director who always entertains, but it’s not much of an apologia for the play itself.
The show ends more in a dribble than a bang.
Both play and production are less challenging, less meaty than they appear.
Alexi Kaye Campbell's play, first seen at The Bush in 2009, is a story of two halves...
Apologia is full of ideas, and its perceptive understanding of both radical ideology and the human heart is an unapologetic success.

For me, for all its skill, Apologia is a fundamentally dishonest play in the sense that the analogy it creates between Kristin’s political activism – her desire to find her voice and save the world – is not automatically antithetical to being a good mother.
The cast unites to create an engaging, lively, revelatory dinner party that the audience members seem delighted to be guests at.
Nevertheless, this is a well-written, very humorous and deeply felt drama...
But director Jamie Lloyd delivers a satisfyingly bumpy ride and it is hard to take your eyes off Channing.

cn.t: Channing delivers a commanding performance as a difficult 1960s radical in Campbell's thought-provoking but heavy-handed family drama about intergenerational conflict and maternal neglect that divides critics.
